# Omni View North America
> **Four hundred thirty-five House seats are on the ballot as voters decide Congress.**

**What You Need to Know:** Voters across the United States began casting ballots Tuesday in midterms that decide which party controls Congress for the last two years of President Trump’s second term. All 435 House seats are up, and Democrats need a net gain of four to take the chamber from a narrow Republican majority. Thirty-five Senate seats are up as well; Republicans hold 53 seats, and Democrats need four gains while holding their own.

### Lead
**Voters head to the polls as control of Congress is on the ballot: The New York Times**
Voters across the United States began heading to the polls on Tuesday in midterms that will decide which party controls Congress for the final two years of President Trump’s second term, the New York Times and The Guardian report. All 435 voting House seats are contested; The Guardian reports Republicans are defending a narrow majority and Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the House. Thirty-five Senate seats are up — 33 in regular elections and special elections in Florida and Ohio — and Republicans hold 53 seats against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them; The Guardian reports Democrats need to gain four seats and defend all of their own to secure a majority. NBC News reports Democrats would have to flip at least two states President Trump won by double digits in 2024. Voters are also choosing governors in 36 states and three US territories, 39 governorships in all, plus thousands of state legislative seats, local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on taxes, abortion rights and voting rules. The New York Times reports Mr. Trump has urged supporters to act as if he is on the ballot and has insisted Republicans would win if his base turned out; Democratic campaigns have blamed the president and his signature policies for household struggles; Republicans have tried to turn the election into a choice against opponents they cast as radical, far-left activists. The Times reports this is the most expensive midterm in political advertising since at least 2018, according to AdImpact, and that Elon Musk contributed $474 million to Republican candidates and their allies. The first polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern; the Times says full results could take days or weeks, and that in 2024 it took three weeks to determine winners in California’s closest House races. A federal judge turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots, and the Supreme Court signaled it was not interested in assisting Mr. Trump’s efforts to interfere with how states administer elections, the Times reports. The Guardian reports the president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterms, a stretch back to 1946. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/03/us/midterms-2026-election-day-trump/heres-the-latest) Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-elections-live-updates-voting) Source: [nbcnews.com](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/senate-results)

### Across the Region
**How a New Brunswick island is caught in the middle of the Canada-U.S. trade war: Global News**
About 900 people live on Campobello Island, New Brunswick, whose only road bridge runs to Lubec, Maine, not to the rest of Canada, Global News reports. There is no gas station on the island and grocery options are limited, so residents cross for basic goods; a student who lives on the island and attends high school in the United States said she crosses the border almost every morning. Residents paid a 25 per cent tariff on US goods brought across the border until Ottawa announced a special exemption for the island. Last month a truckload of supplies was turned back by US border officials, and a Campobello brewery has shut down because of the tariffs. Canadian tourism to Maine was cut in half last year following President Trump’s taunts and tariffs. New Brunswick MP John Williamson said decisions made in distant capitals hit Campobello immediately; Lubec resident Nelson Meaker said there is no reason to cause bad blood among good neighbours. American fisherman Dana Barker, who has lived on the island with his Canadian wife for 50 years, said the two sides will work it out. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12130717/island-caught-canada-u-s-tensions-midterms-campobello-nb/)

**Maine Senate pits Susan Collins against Troy Jackson: PBS**
Maine’s Senate election pits incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president, PBS reports. Collins, first elected in 1996, is seeking a sixth term; PBS reports she is the only Republican senator from a state Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election, and that she won by nine points in 2020 when polls showed her losing. Oyster farmer Graham Platner won the Democratic primary by a landslide in June, then dropped out a month later after sexual assault allegations emerged. A party convention then chose Jackson, a former logger whose campaign has centered on working-class economics. Source: [pbs.org](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-maine-senate-midterm-election)

**Ukrainian truckers who fled war swept up in immigration stops: The New York Times**
At least a dozen Ukrainian truck drivers were arrested this summer, according to a representative for Ukraine, and several remain in detention, the New York Times reports. On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officers across 15 states had stopped more than 1,000 commercial trucks and arrested about 40 immigrant drivers, including some with serious criminal charges. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/ukraine-immigrant-trucker-cdl-weigh-stations-ice.html)

### The Closer Look
**Ohio’s Senate, governor and House races on a right-shifted map: PBS**
Voters in Ohio are choosing a US senator in a special election, a governor, and the state’s 15 US House seats on Tuesday, in a state the Associated Press, via PBS, describes as having shifted sharply toward the right over the last decade. Polls close at 7:30 p.m. Eastern. For Democrats nationally, PBS reports, Ohio may be crucial to a bid to retake Congress.

Republican Jon Husted faces Democrat Sherrod Brown for the Senate seat. Husted was appointed in 2025 by Republican Governor Mike DeWine to fill the vacancy JD Vance left when he became vice president. The winner serves the remaining two years of that term. Brown held Ohio’s other Senate seat for three terms until 2025, when Republican Bernie Moreno defeated him in a tight race. President Trump carried Ohio in the last three presidential elections, and Republicans have controlled the governor’s office and the state Legislature for more than a decade. Husted has the president’s endorsement.

The cost of living has been a core issue. Brown has tied Trump’s war in Iran to climbing gas prices and attacked Husted for repeated votes against war-powers resolutions that could have directed the president to end the conflict. In September, Husted said the war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so gas prices can be lowered. Brown has labeled Husted “the face of data centers,” a reference to Husted’s support for data-center projects as lieutenant governor, a post he held until 2025. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted could lose because of data centers.

# Omni View North America

> **Democrats won both the House and the Senate, ending Republican control of Congress.**

**What You Need to Know:** Democrats won both the House and the Senate, ending Republican control of Congress and, as The New York Times reported, the party's hold on the House, the Senate and the presidency together. President Trump attributed the losses to his name not being on the ballot; The New York Times reported that others in his party dismissed that explanation and blamed him. The same night reset governor's offices from Texas outward, put a Canadian submarine purchase back in play, and put Hakeem Jeffries in line to lead the House.

### Lead
**Democrats Seize Control of Congress, Ending a G.O.P. Trifecta: The New York Times**
The New York Times reported that the Democratic Party wrested control of Congress from Republicans, and that Republicans lost both the House and the Senate, in what the paper called a wave of midterm victories and a stinging rebuke to President Trump's agenda. The Times reported that the House result ended a Republican trifecta and cemented divided government and a freshly assertive Congress after two years in which, the paper wrote, Republicans ceded power to President Trump. In a separate account, the Times reported that the backlash extended even into deep red states and, in the paper's reading, indicated that President Trump has lost his hold over the coalition that lifted him to the White House twice. The Times also reported a string of Senate victories in Iowa, Texas, and North and South Carolina, and wrote that Democrats flipped the Senate and the House with ease, leaving the president weakened. President Trump attributed the sweeping losses to the fact that he was not on the ballot. The Times reported that others in his party dismissed that explanation and pinned the blame squarely on him. He told the Times, "There was a mood in the air, I guess." On Truth Social, the BBC reported, he wrote that Republicans would have won "in a landslide" if his name had been on the ballot. The BBC's account was headlined that he takes aim at Republicans but says Democrats did a "good job." Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/midterm-election-photos.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/democratic-midterms-wipeout.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/elections/house-of-representatives-midterms-democrats-republicans.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/trump-republicans-blame-midterms.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/election-takeaways-democrats-win.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/midterm-election-rebuke-of-trump-era.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/politics/senate-election-control.html) Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6073l9y15xxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

### Across the Region
**Gina Hinojosa Wins Texas Governor Race in Major Upset, Defeating Greg Abbott: The New York Times**
The New York Times reported that State Representative Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, denying him a fourth term, and that she is the first Hispanic candidate elected to lead Texas. The Times reported she concentrated on pocketbook issues, and that voters' opposition to Republican immigration policies was a tailwind. The same paper reported that victories by James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa upended decades of statewide Republican dominance in what had been the nation's most populous conservative state, a shift the Times described as once unthinkable. The paper called the night a Democratic rout that stunned Texas. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/texas-governor-abbott-hinojosa.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/gina-hinojosa-texas-governor.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/texas-talarico-hinojosa-abbott-paxton.html)

**Canada looking to Germany for 8 submarines up front and 4 later: sources: CBC**
Canada is looking to split a planned purchase of twelve German submarines, committing to eight up front and leaving the remaining four for a future decision, sources told CBC News. CBC reported the proposal is intended to preserve financial flexibility. Those sources said the split could jeopardize some of the eighty-six billion dollars in economic benefits promised by Germany. The figures and the split come from sources speaking to CBC, not from a signed contract described in the report. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-germany-submarines-defence-industry-economy-9.7407952?cmp=rss) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-germany-submarines-defence-industry-economy-9.7407952)

**Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House: NPR**
NPR reported that Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House after House control was called for Democrats. As speaker he would be second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president. He has vowed to focus on affordability and on holding the administration accountable. Addressing supporters, he argued that voters sent Congress a message to end extremism and "corruption." NPR headlined that he declares "America is back." The New York Times reported he would make history as the first Black speaker, and, in a separate account of what to know about him, that he was raised by a Black nationalist family in Brooklyn, is a moderate, and loves a hip-hop reference. The Times also reported that he told supporters, "We Hear You." Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/g-s1-150030/hakeem-jeffries-speaker-of-the-house-midterms) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028572/hakeem-jeffries-midterms-house) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/hakeem-jeffries-what-to-know.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/hakeem-jeffries-house.html)

### The Closer Look
**Public menopause care is scarce, and private care is costly. Why Canadians pay either way: The Globe and Mail**
Angela Rimmer has spent more than five thousand dollars out of pocket on menopause care that Ontario does not cover. She is forty-two, a single mother of four in the London, Ontario, area, and a full-time dental assistant. She told The Globe and Mail that brain fog, difficulty sleeping, night sweats, hot flashes, mood changes and exhaustion were debilitating, and that she needed treatment to keep working and to keep caregiving at home. A family doctor initially misdiagnosed her and wanted to prescribe antidepressants. She turned to two different private clinics for menopause hormone therapy. At one clinic she paid six hundred dollars for an initial assessment, two hundred dollars for each six-month follow-up, seventy dollars for lab tests, and about one hundred and twenty dollars a month in prescriptions. She has no private health insurance, and the province does not cover the treatments. She said, "I just wish that I didn't have to access this through private. I wish that it was in the public system, because we're having to pay so much." She said access, including the hormone therapy that has helped her, should be available without reaching so far into pocketbooks at the time when women should be saving for retirement and for their children's schooling. Private care, she said, has been costly and time-consuming to find.

The Globe and Mail reported that more than five million women in Canada are between forty and sixty, and that the majority will experience menopause symptoms, which can run from mild to overwhelming. Symptoms the paper listed range from fatigue to headaches, anxiety, muscle aches and heart palpitations. An Ipsos survey this year for GreenShield found that four in ten Canadian women do not know where to go for treatment, and that a third of respondents waited more than two years to get effective menopause care. The paper listed the barriers as a shortage of family physicians, doctors who lack training in menopause, long waits to see specialists, a dearth of research funding, and an explosion of misleading information online. Desperate for treatment, some women turn to private or virtual clinics. Some are run by physicians or nurse practitioners; others are operated by naturopaths or tech entrepreneurs. Women's health experts told the paper that the standard of care varies, and so do the prices, that many remedies are costly, and that not all are effective or safe. The paper reported that effective treatments exist that alleviate symptoms, and that most cases are not so complex that a family doctor cannot handle them. Currently, just two provinces, British Columbia and Manitoba, cover the costs of menopausal hormone therapy. Newer nonhormonal medications, Veozah and Lynkuet, which alleviate hot flashes and night sweats, are approved by Health Canada but are not fully covered by the public system. The Globe and Mail reported that Canada is behind Britain and Australia in taking steps to improve access. In June, the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada warned that a two-tiered health system is emerging in which women are forced to pay for basic health care that should be free.

The Menopause Foundation of Canada says access should be universally available to all Canadians. It started a national campaign last month urging governments to bolster support for women experiencing menopause. The foundation says the widest gaps are for Indigenous, Black and racialized women, people living in rural communities, gender-diverse people and those with lower incomes. It said, "Access to safe, evidence-based menopause care should never depend on a person's ability to pay." Gynecologist and author Jen Gunter, of The Menopause Manifesto, said that whether someone lives in Flin Flon, Manitoba, or in downtown Toronto, they should be able to get excellent first-line menopause care, just as people should have access to care for blood pressure, and that these are things that should be available to everybody. In Lindsay, Ontario, Monika Kerschl-Sales, co-owner of Thairapy Beauty Bar, said she hears about menopause all the time, and that hundreds of women in the region who sit in her stylist chair have shared their struggles in getting care. She described her own perimenopause — low moods, fatigue, hot flashes, night sweats and brain fog — as a stretch when she did not feel like herself and could not bring her best to work. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-menopause-health-care-public-private-clinics-costs/)

### Also Today
**Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeats Republican Mike Rogers in key Michigan Senate race: NPR**
Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race after a campaign NPR described as testing an antiestablishment candidate on the left in a perennial Midwest battleground, and with the win he will be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate. Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine, NPR reported, flipping a Senate seat she had held for nearly thirty years and ending three decades in the Senate for the sole Republican representing New England in Congress, as The New York Times put it. PBS reported that Democrat Christina Bohannan won election to the U.S. House in Iowa's 1st Congressional District, and The New York Times reported she unseated Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, with discontent about the war with Iran and tariffs helping create a tough environment for the defeated Republican. In Nackawic, New Brunswick, the pulp mill across the river emitted what might have been its last puff of smoke last week, and the town's largest employer for half a century is shutting down because of "prevailing market conditions," according to the India-based owner, AV Group New Brunswick. # Omni View North America
> **Democrats gained two hundred fifty-eight statehouse seats, resetting who writes law in state capitals.**

**What You Need to Know:** Democrats gained 258 state legislative seats in Tuesday’s midterms, according to State Navigate, resetting who holds chambers and governorships across the United States. Two Senate races were still uncalled, including Mississippi, where Scott Colom led Cindy Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes and the state has no recount law. In Canada, Mark Carney tables a second budget on Thursday that a Fraser Institute commentator says deepens deficits younger taxpayers will carry.

### Lead
**Democrats Gain Hundreds of State Legislative Seats: The Guardian**
Democrats gained 258 state legislative seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, according to Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of State Navigate, creating six new governing trifectas, taking 11 legislative chambers from Republicans and breaking Republican supermajorities in 10 states. The Guardian reports that ballots are still being counted, and that the party has not held full control of government in Arizona in 60 years, in Pennsylvania since the 1990s, or in Wisconsin since 2010, while Michigan and Minnesota regained trifectas lost after the 2024 election. In Texas, Democrats will control the state house for the first time since 2002. The New York Times reports they won control of state governments in Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Nevada, and won chambers in Texas, Georgia and North Carolina. They also won gubernatorial races over Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010, the Guardian reports. Mandara Meyers, executive director of the States Project, said it was the most significant night for state legislative power since the Republican wave of 2010, and that Democrats now have more power in the states than at any other point in the 21st century. Nuttycombe predicts about 76 percent of the population will live under a Democratic governor and about half will be represented by a Democratic lawmaker in their legislature, and he said roughly 80 to 85 percent of the wave is the economy and dissatisfaction with the president. The Guardian says Democrats are on course for a Senate majority of at least 54 seats and 237 House seats. Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan, leaders of the Democratic Governors Association, said more Democratic governors mean better lives for the millions of Americans who live in their states. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/05/democrats-state-legislatures-midterm-elections) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/state-legislatures-democrats-midterm-election.html)

### Across the Region
**Mississippi Senate Race Leads by 1,138 Votes, and the State Has No Recount Law: The Guardian**
Almost 24 hours after Democrats secured control of Congress, two Senate seats were still in play, with counting in Alaska expected to continue into Thursday. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes with almost 96 percent counted, the Guardian reports, and new batches had not been reported for several hours even as Colom’s votes had been outpacing hers. Mississippi has no law for initiating a recount; The New York Times reports the state does not allow vote recounts in statewide elections. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024, and the state has not elected a Black person to that office since 1875. Colom, a seventh-generation Mississippian whose father was a Republican, became the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit in 2015 and, as district attorney, had a 94 percent success rate for convictions. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/05/midterm-elections-live-latest-updates-mississippi-senate-race) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/mississippi-senate-election-recount-law.html)

**Triumphal Arch Set to Win Final Approval Despite Court Challenges: The New York Times**
After court challenges to the project, a federal planning board is expected to give final approval on Thursday to President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch, The New York Times reports. NPR reports the panel meets Thursday and the government said it may begin construction later that same day. Critics hope a judge will intervene at the last minute. The Times reports court action and Democrats’ upcoming control of Congress could halt the plans. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/us/politics/trump-triumphal-arch-planning-commission.html) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-6027301/trump-arch-federal-approval-judge-construction)

### The Closer Look
**What to watch for as Carney introduces his 2nd federal budget: CBC**
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government tables its second federal budget on Thursday, since taking office in March 2025. The CBC says the budget is the next step in a plan to support the country through an affordability crunch and the trade war. A Globe and Mail headline in the same day’s coverage says Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said the budget will focus on affordability and cultural sovereignty.

Jake Fuss, director of fiscal studies at the Fraser Institute, argues in The Globe and Mail that Canadians should expect more new spending and large deficits. He writes that Carney promised on the campaign trail a “very different approach” to federal finances from Justin Trudeau, and later said he would be “spending less,” then increased spending significantly. Fuss says the government posted a $66.9-billion deficit for 2025-26, a projected deficit of $65.3-billion in 2026-27, and deficits of at least $53-billion for each of the subsequent four years. Those cumulative deficits from 2025-26 to 2029-30, he writes, are double what Trudeau planned before leaving office. Ottawa has not balanced a budget in nearly 20 years, he notes, after the Trudeau government borrowed hundreds of billions and pushed inflation-adjusted per-person spending and debt to historically high levels.

To cover the deficit, Ottawa must borrow. Fuss says total federal debt will eclipse a projected $2.9-trillion by 2029-30 — almost $300-billion more than Trudeau planned — and that debt interest costs will hit a projected $75.7-billion, more than the combined total Ottawa plans to spend that year on employment insurance and the Canada Child Benefit. He argues the burden lands disproportionately on younger Canadians, who are likely to pay higher taxes, enjoy fewer services, or both. He also argues that when the government borrows, it competes with individuals, families and businesses, and that lenders raise interest rates, making mortgages, cars and renovations more expensive. He says today’s higher interest rates exist in part because of federal and provincial spending and borrowing.

Last year, Fuss writes, the Carney government separated “operating spending” — day-to-day programs such as Old Age Security and employment insurance — from “capital spending,” defined as “anything that builds an asset,” and said last month it would balance the operating budget by 2028-29. He says both categories affect the bottom line, and that the split obscures the true state of federal finances. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has criticized how the government classifies capital spending, he writes, because the government has an incentive to shift items from operating to capital. A separate PBO report last month said the government is not on track to balance the operating budget by 2028-29 regardless of that classification. Fuss’s conclusion is that, absent substantial spending reductions or huge jumps in revenue, the overall deficit remains larger than the Trudeau government’s projections, and that younger Canadians inherit the bill. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/carney-second-federal-budget-lookahead-9.7409464?cmp=rss) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/commentary/article-carney-federal-budget-younger-canadians-will-pay-for-massive-spending/)

### Also Today
**Some Americans Turn to Libraries as Prices Stay High: NPR**
NPR reports some Americans squeezed by high prices are relying more on local libraries for books, streaming services and high-priced items such as musical instruments and sewing machines. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-5992908/libraries-and-cost-of-living)

**A Democratic Congress Would Struggle to Move Fuel Prices Directly: NPR**
NPR reports a new Democratic majority could pressure the president to end the war in Iran, but fuel prices are tied to a complex international oil market and will be harder for Congress to affect directly. # Omni View North America
> **Governor Newsom commuted all five hundred forty-eight California death sentences, a quarter of the national total.**

**What You Need to Know:** Governor Newsom commuted all five hundred forty-eight California death sentences, a quarter of the national total. He called capital punishment morally objectionable, and California has not carried out an execution in twenty years. The Times reports he is considering a presidential run; Austin Sarat writes in The Guardian that emptying death row frees hundreds from the threat of execution.

### Lead
**Newsom Commutes the Sentences of California’s 548 Death Row Inmates: The New York Times**
Governor Gavin Newsom commuted the sentences of California’s 548 people on death row, The New York Times reports. He called capital punishment morally objectionable. The Times reports he is considering a run for president, and that California has not executed anyone for 20 years. Those 548 sentences are about a quarter of death sentences nationwide, the Times reports. In The Guardian, Austin Sarat writes that the decision to empty the state’s death row frees hundreds of people from the threat of execution. Sarat, treating Newsom as a politician who may seek the presidency, argues that the move signals opposition to the death penalty is no longer a third rail in US politics. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/us/california-death-row-newsom-commutation.html) Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/06/california-gavin-newsom-death-row-history)

### Across the Region
**Carney's bet on economic growth — and the risks that come with it: CBC**
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s budget bets that Ottawa can borrow billions now for major projects meant to jump-start the economy, CBC reports, and CBC says a failed payoff would leave Canada’s debt load exposed to new risks. Bloomberg reports the budget spends an oil windfall on housing and investment measures. On defence, CBC reports a path to 157 billion dollars in annual spending by 2030, closer to NATO’s five per cent target, with few details on rearmament and no roadmap past 2030. The Globe and Mail reports Ottawa is easing off defence increases, with no further progress toward the military spending target beyond 2027-28, while CBC says analysts question whether fiscal pressure and shifting priorities will undermine the commitments. Leaders of the Bloc Québécois, the NDP and the Green Party told The Globe and Mail the budget was disappointing, lacked substance and did not do enough on affordability. The Globe and Mail also reports a 4 billion dollar cultural-sector boost for national museums, art galleries, journalism and a new national digital library, framed as support for national sovereignty. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/armstrong-canada-budget-2026-economy-risks-9.7411557?cmp=rss) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/defence-budget-military-nato-trump-9.7411329?cmp=rss) Source: [bloomberg.com](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-11-05/canada-budget-2026-carney-spends-oil-windfall-on-tax-measures-housing-plan) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-federal-budget-defence-spending-2026-canada/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/video-opposition-leaders-react-to-2026-budget/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-federal-budget-2026-canada-culture-national-identity-sovereignty/)

**A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval: NPR**
A day after the triumphal arch sat on the verge of approval, a federal judge blocked construction for 14 days, NPR reports, moments after a federal panel approved it late Thursday. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the hold while the court weighs legality; NPR reports the administration had hoped to start at once, and the order came just after midnight. Euronews reports the National Capital Planning Commission approved a 250-foot arch, inspired by Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, beside Arlington National Cemetery. Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat, told the commission the arch would dishonour America and disrupt the link between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery, and he called it a tribute to Donald Trump. Greg Wischer of the Interior Department said it would fulfil a 100-year plan for a monumental work on Columbia Island. President Trump has said the structure would become a top-grade military complex to house drones, snipers and ammunition, Euronews reports. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6031990/trump-arch-planning-commission-injunction) Source: [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/06/judge-blocks-construction-of-trumps-massive-triumphal-arch)

**1 Officer Is Killed and 3 Are Wounded in Shootout on Suburban Denver Bus: The New York Times**
One police officer was killed and three were wounded after a man opened fire on officers who pursued him onto a bus in Lakewood, Colorado, The New York Times reports, citing the authorities. A civilian was also injured. The authorities said police shot the gunman dead. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/lakewood-police-shooting-colorado-bus-dead.html)

### The Closer Look
**Online gambling more than doubles among young Montreal men, study finds: Global News**
Online gambling has more than doubled among men aged 18 to 34 in Montreal, even as the share of adults who gamble at all has fallen, Global News reports from a new public health study. Researchers surveyed 8,500 Montreal adults. Thirty-nine per cent said they had gambled in some form in 2025, 15 per cent fewer than in 2018 and in 2002. The authors say the line runs the other way for younger men: the number who reported gambling online has more than doubled.

Sylvia Kairouz, a Concordia University gambling researcher and one of the authors, said the phone is the mechanism. When a person only has to pick up a phone and push a button, she said, resisting is very difficult. She said researchers have seen more interest in online gambling than in casinos or any other physical location.

Anne Elizabeth Lapointe, chief executive of Maison Jean Lapointe, which offers treatment for gambling addiction, said the study matches the people coming through the door. She told Global News on Thursday that more and more young men are seeking help for online gambling addiction. Since the COVID pandemic, she said, the organization has been helping far fewer people struggling with in-person slots or video lottery terminals, while online gambling has become the growing concern. She said even minors are finding ways to gamble online. For the last two years, she said, kids have come to the office with a gambling addiction or with serious consequences from the habit, and young people with little or no income can face serious consequences from their losses.

The earlier steps the sources name are that pandemic-era shift away from physical machines, and the spread of advertising. Kairouz said the volume of gambling advertising is making sports betting more socially acceptable. The study found 75 per cent of those surveyed wished there were no advertisements at all for gambling sites. Lapointe said gambling advertising needs to be banned or regulated more effectively.

The figures land on men 18 to 34, on minors who reach the sites, and on the clinics treating them. For anyone who still bets, Kairouz recommends setting a budget and sticking to it. She said that over the long term, people who bet on sports will lose money because unpredictable outcomes are unavoidable, and that the house always wins. Help is available across Canada for gambling-related problems. In Quebec, Gambling: Help and Referral offers free, confidential support around the clock, in Montreal and elsewhere in the province, including online. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12139130/online-gambling-betting-doubles-montreal-men/)

Tenants at an apartment building in Edmonton’s McCauley neighbourhood have gone a week without working water and heat, Global News reports, in a building that shows disrepair outside and evidence of drug use inside. The Guardian reports nine Edmonton Oilers games this season, and a handful of games for each Canadian NHL team, are available only with a 12.99 dollar monthly Sportsnet+ subscription from Rogers, with some other games only on Amazon Prime. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/nov/06/hockeys-streaming-spree-means-theres-one-fewer-thing-holding-canada-together)

### Both Sides: Whether a president can lock the Oval Office as a national monument
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order declaring the Oval Office a national monument, and the fight is over whether that order can stop a successor from altering it. Trump’s case, as he put it to reporters, is that the room is a symbol of the country and should not be touched, destroyed or ripped down by a later president in order to build something in a slightly different shape. He said the White House and the Oval Office had been badly damaged before his changes, describing broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone, and he said the order would make it impossible for anybody to destroy the space.

The order’s own text, as the BBC reports it, cuts the other way: it does not restrict a president’s authority to redecorate, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security changes that do not substantially impair the historic structure. Greg Werkheiser, of the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, told the BBC that furniture and decor are already up to the president so long as permanent art and architecture are not damaged, and he called the order legally meaningless because Trump cannot bind a successor this way. Werkheiser called it hypocrisy beside the demolition of the East Wing, a project the BBC reports was not approved by Congress and is continuing as a ballroom, and beside what he described as lawsuits aimed at weakening preservation law. The grounds are already a National Historic Landmark. Trump himself scaled back two national monuments in Utah in 2017, and the BBC reports that revoking a monument designation has not been tested in court, so it is unclear whether a future president or a lawsuit could undo this order. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy0eeg101djo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

# Omni View North America
> **Stephen Miller replaces Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, sharpening Trump's immigration line.**

**What You Need to Know:** Stephen Miller is the new White House chief of staff after President Donald Trump, on Friday afternoon, said on Truth Social that Miller would replace Susie Wiles and confirmed she had been ousted. The Guardian describes Miller as Trump's most trusted adviser and as the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, and it reports the change in the wake of the midterm elections. The Guardian says Democrats and Republicans criticized the promotion, and that Democratic lawmakers called Miller a hatemonger, a xenophobe and vile.

### Lead
**Trump faces criticism for ‘dangerous’ Stephen Miller appointment as White House chief of staff: The Guardian US**
On Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump abruptly announced on his Truth Social platform that Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, and he confirmed that Wiles had been ousted. The Guardian describes Miller as Trump's most trusted adviser. It also describes him as the architect of Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, the record the appointment puts at the center of the West Wing. The Guardian places the announcement in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections. It reports that Democrats and Republicans criticized the promotion. Democratic lawmakers, the Guardian reports, decried Miller as a hatemonger, a xenophobe and vile. The criticism, as the Guardian presents it, is aimed at the person now running the White House staff operation, not at a proposal still awaiting a decision. For the immigration apparatus Miller has led, the change puts that adviser in the chief of staff's chair after the midterms rather than leaving Wiles in the post. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-democrats-react)

### Across the Region
**Canada's military is using Palantir software. What are the risks?: CBC Politics**
Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with the U.S. technology firm Palantir, and the Canadian military is using the company's software. Experts warn that the deals could expose military data to U.S. authorities. They also warn that the contracts could deepen Canada's reliance on foreign technology. The Department of National Defence says its systems keep government data secure in Canada. The dispute, as CBC reports it, is over where that data can be reached and how dependent the military becomes, not over whether the contracts exist. For Canadian defence systems that now run on Palantir software, the experts' warning and the department's assurance are the two accounts on the table. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/palantir-canadian-military-9.7409099?cmp=rss)

**Mysterious Request Scrambles Major Supreme Court Gun Case Against Cook County: The New York Times US**
The lead plaintiff in one of two cases challenging semiautomatic weapons bans has asked to drop out, the New York Times reports. The request comes weeks before the cases are heard. The Times calls the move unusual. It says the request scrambles a major Supreme Court case against Cook County. The case is one of two on those bans, so the withdrawal request hits the lead plaintiff in a paired set of challenges rather than a lone filing. For Cook County's semiautomatic weapons ban, the Times reports that the challenge reaching the Court has been scrambled before argument by the plaintiff's own request to leave the case. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/us/politics/supreme-court-guns-plaintiff.html)

**Houston Police to Stop Alerting ICE During Traffic Stops: The New York Times US**
Mayor John Whitmire has instructed Houston police to stop notifying immigration agents when they encounter someone without legal status during routine street stops, the New York Times reports. The instruction applies to those routine street stops, not to a broader rewrite of federal immigration law. Houston officers, under the mayor's order, are no longer to alert Immigration and Customs Enforcement in that encounter. For people without legal status stopped on Houston streets, the change is in whether local police make that notification. The Times attributes the instruction to Whitmire. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/houston-mayor-john-whitmire-immigration-ice-cooperation.html)

### The Closer Look
**One of Okanagan’s most colourful characters dies at 96: Global News Canada**
Eddy Haymour died on Wednesday at the age of 96. For decades, a distinctive castle overlooking Highway 97 in Peachland has served as a reminder of him. Global News reports that he leaves a story of ambition, controversy and a dream that never quite came to fruition. For many locals, his name is synonymous with both the castle and Rattlesnake Island. Okanagan resident Don Scramstad put it this way: “Rattlesnake island and a bit of trouble, a lot of trouble.”

Haymour, a Lebanese immigrant, purchased Rattlesnake Island in 1971 with plans to transform the five-acre property into a Middle Eastern-themed amusement park. That vision caught the attention of filmmaker Greg Crompton, who produced the 2019 documentary “Eddy’s Kingdom.” Crompton told Global News that, when ideas were being kicked around, this one seemed a compelling story to tell. “So I was quite motivated personally but also as a filmmaker, I want to tell interesting stories. This is a very interesting story,” Crompton said.

The dispute with the provincial government escalated in 1974, when Haymour and his relatives took hostages at the Canadian embassy in Beirut. Crompton said Haymour’s rationale was the most interesting part of him, and described a thought process in Haymour’s own framing: wronged by the government, then “you were going to get some grenades and chuck it into the legislature and and cause mayhem.” Crompton said that thought process was maybe the most compelling part. At the Peachland Museum, Haymour remains a prominent figure in the community’s history. Assistant curator Jeff Green said, “He was zealously committed to his dream,” and that it did not matter what obstacle was in his way; he pursued it to the end.

Haymour eventually won his legal battle with the province. His dream of developing the island never materialized. He did build the castle in Peachland, and beside it a statue of himself pointing across the lake toward the island he had big dreams for. Tracy Janes, a customer service agent at the museum, said, “He was a visionary. He was impassioned about what he was doing,” and that everything about the man was larger than life. For Peachland, the castle on Highway 97 and the statue aimed at Rattlesnake Island are what remain of a five-acre plan from 1971, a 1974 hostage-taking in Beirut, a legal win against the province, and a development that never rose on the island. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12140696/okanagans-colourful-character-dies-96-eddy-haymour/)

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is pressing G7 allies to intensify pressure on Russia after an attack on a Ukrainian aid distribution site killed 53 people. Anand says the international community must strengthen sanctions and military support. She says allies should confront Moscow directly when world leaders gather for December’s G20 summit in Florida. The strike she is answering killed 53 people at an aid distribution site in Ukraine; the pressure she is asking for runs through the G7 and toward that Florida meeting. For Canada’s place in those rooms, Anand is tying a civilian death toll she cites to sanctions, military support, and a direct confrontation with Moscow in December. **U.S. Homeless Population Had Record Drop in 2025: The New York Times US**
The Department of Housing and Urban Development reported a record drop in the U.S. homeless population in 2025. HUD credited President Trump. Homeless advocacy groups said that so-called Housing First policies of his predecessors played a part. The Times presents both accounts of the same reported drop: the department’s credit to the current president, and the groups’ credit to earlier Housing First policy. For people counted in that population, the reported change is a record decline in 2025, with the cause still disputed between HUD and those advocacy groups.
